summary: Describes the Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable throughput (L4S) architecture. It rests on the idea that queuing delay is caused by capacity-seeking congestion controllers at senders, not by the queue itself, and it lets applications transition to scalable congestion control for very low delay. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: L4S is an architecture for keeping network queues short while sending data quickly. It asks senders to respond to congestion signals more often, and gives network equipment a way to separate this traffic from traffic using older congestion controls.

what is a scalable congestion control
subtitle: How senders and networks can keep queues short while sharing a bottleneck link.

tldr.problem: Congestion-control behavior at senders can create large queue swings and long delays, even when networks use active queue management.
tldr.mechanism: L4S combines scalable congestion control at senders, network treatment that separates L4S from Classic traffic, and ECN signaling that identifies L4S packets.
tldr.outcome: The architecture aims for low queuing delay and loss while allowing L4S and Classic traffic to share a network. It is described here; related protocol mechanisms are specified in RFC 9331 and RFC 9332.

today: RFC 9330 is an Informational RFC published in January 2023. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes an architecture, while related mechanisms are specified in RFC 9331 and RFC 9332.

sections.title: Why Queues Create Delay
sections.content:
When a network link is busy, packets wait in a queue. This waiting can add substantial and variable delay to interactive applications. The RFC explains that simply making queues shallower can reduce link use for existing congestion controls.

Its central claim is that sender behavior contributes to queue growth. L4S is intended to let applications use congestion controls that respond to signals without building the larger queues associated with Classic controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets wait when too much data reaches a busy link at once. L4S changes how senders react so they can use the link without keeping a long line of waiting packets.

sections.title: The Three Parts of L4S
sections.content:
The architecture has three components: a scalable congestion control in the sending host, network support that isolates L4S traffic from Classic traffic, and a protocol signal that lets network devices identify the traffic.

The sender's congestion control is responsible for keeping its queue use low. The network helps protect that low delay and signals the start of queue growth using Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN).
sections.plainLanguage: A sender adjusts its rate, network equipment separates traffic treatments, and an IP header signal identifies L4S packets. These parts work together; the network alone does not create the low delay.

sections.title: Network and Host Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC describes the ECN codepoint ECT(1) as the L4S identifier and CE as a congestion signal. A Dual-Queue Coupled Active Queue Management system can place L4S and Classic packets in separate queues while coupling their congestion signals.

Other approaches include per-flow queues or dual queues with per-flow marking. A sender also needs scalable congestion control and suitable feedback from the receiver. Requirements vary by transport protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Network equipment can place identified L4S packets in a separate queue and mark packets when congestion begins. The sender must understand the marks and adjust its sending rate.

sections.title: Deployment and Security
sections.content:
L4S is designed for incremental deployment. The RFC discusses deploying support at bottleneck links and explains that a flow may need a scalable sender, a suitable queue-management system, and accurate receiver feedback.

The security discussion considers traffic that does not respond properly to congestion and traffic that could disrupt the low-delay queue. It lists possible network protections, including per-flow queue protection and traffic conditioning.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can add L4S support in stages, but each part of the path must handle the signals correctly for a flow to receive the intended treatment. The RFC also describes ways operators can protect the shared queue from unresponsive traffic.

references.text: The Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Protocol for Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S), RFC 9331.
